topic: Why Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is critical supply chain defense, not just compliance theater
post_text:
Most security teams treat SBOM as a checkbox—a document to generate and file away. That misses the entire point.

I'm talking about what an SBOM actually does: it gives you visibility into every component, dependency, and transitive library bundled into your software. When a vulnerability drops, you can answer "Do we use this?" in minutes instead of days.

The 2024 MOVEit Transfer RCE (CVE-2024-34498) showed exactly why. Progress Software patched a critical SQL injection in their file transfer product, but organizations couldn't quickly determine if they were exposed because they had no inventory of their own third-party dependencies—let alone what MOVEit itself contained.

Now consider the opposite: organizations running mature SBOM practices (cycloneDX or SPDX format) could:
• Run their SBOM through a vulnerability scanner in real-time
• Identify affected versions within hours
• Prioritize patching based on actual exposure

Here's what's widely missed: SBOM isn't primarily about preventing breaches. It's about reducing mean time to detection and response when supply chain vulnerabilities surface. That difference is measured in millions of dollars of dwell time.

The U.S. Executive Order 14028 and the NIST SSDF framework mandated SBOMs for good reason—they're the foundation of rational risk decision-making in modern software supply chains.

If you're not generating SBOMs, you're running blind on your own attack surface.

♻️ Repost if this helped someone.
